q: The word 'ethics' comes from the Greek 'ethos', meaning what?
explain: Ethos [Greek] meaning custom or character.

q: Which of the following statements about ethics is correct?
options: Ethics are a type of company policy
Ethics are always the same as the law
Ethics are not necessarily the law
Ethics are the same for everyone
explain: Ethics are not necessarily the law and not the same for everyone.

q: Who may have been the first proponent of ethical behavior?
explain: Hippocrates may have been the first proponent of ethical behavior.

q: What is the FIRST thing to do before you make an ethical decision?
options: List the consequences of the actions
explain: The list begins: clearly identify all the facts, define the areas of potential conflict, identify the stakeholders, list all options, list the consequences, now make the decision.

q: In the steps before making an ethical decision, what comes immediately after 'Clearly identify all the facts'?
options: Define the areas of potential conflict
explain: Order on the slide: facts, areas of potential conflict, stakeholders, options, consequences, decision.

q: In the steps before making an ethical decision, what is done immediately BEFORE listing the consequences of the actions?
options: Define the areas of potential conflict
explain: Options are listed, then the consequences of the actions are listed, then the decision is made.

q: Which principle says: take the decision for the greatest good of everyone?
explain: Utilitarianism Principle: take the decision for the greatest good of everyone.

q: Which principle says: take the decision that causes least harm?
explain: Risk Aversion Principle: take the decision that causes least harm.

q: The Rule of Universality ('if the action is not right for everyone, then it is not right for anyone') is attributed to whom?
explain: Rule of Universality (Kant, 1724-1804).

q: Which rule says: if an action cannot be taken repeatedly, then it is not right to take it at all?
explain: Rule of Change: if an action cannot be taken repeatedly, then it is not right to take it at all (Descartes, 1596-1650).
flag: Slide attributes the Rule of Change to Descartes (1596-1650); follow the slide.

q: Which philosopher is named alongside the Rule of Change?
explain: Rule of Change ... (Descartes, 1596-1650); Rule of Universality is Kant, 1724-1804.

q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a source of ethics?
explain: Slide lists Supernaturalism, Intuitionism, Consequentialism, Exemplars, Ideologies.

q: Which ethical position is expressed by 'I disapprove of murder'?
explain: Subjectivism - 'I disapprove of murder'.

q: Which ethical position is expressed by 'don't murder'?
explain: Prescriptivism - 'don't murder'.

q: Which ethical position is expressed by 'down with murder'?
explain: Emotivism - 'down with murder'.

q: How does the lecture sum up a person's morals?
options: The decisions they make under legal pressure
The rules laid down by a governing body
The collection of the environmental factors they are exposed to and what they have taken away from them
The code of conduct of their professional body
explain: A person's morals can be summed up as 'the collection of the environmental factors they are exposed to and what they have taken away from them.'

q: In the prisoner theory game, what happens if A and B each betray the other?
options: Each serves one year in prison
Each serves two years in prison
Each serves three years in prison
explain: If A and B each betray the other, each of them serves two years in prison.

q: In the prisoner theory game, A betrays B but B remains silent. What happens?
options: A is set free and B serves three years
A serves three years and B is set free
explain: If A betrays B but B remains silent, A will be set free and B will serve three years in prison.

q: In the prisoner theory game, what happens if A and B both remain silent?
options: Both serve only one year (on the lesser charge)
One is set free and the other serves three years
explain: If A and B both remain silent, both of them will only serve one year in prison (on the lesser charge).

q: What does prisoner theory show?
options: Rational people always cooperate when they cannot communicate
Betrayal is never the rational choice
Two completely rational people might not cooperate, even when it is in their best interests to do so
explain: Prisoner theory shows that two completely rational people might not cooperate ... even when its is in their best interests to do so.

q: In the prisoner theory scenario, what charge do the prosecutors lack enough evidence to convict the pair on?
options: Breach of the Data Protection Act
explain: Prosecutors lack sufficient evidence to convict the pair on the principal charge of hacking, but have enough to convict both on a lesser charge.

q: Which of the following is NOT a trait of an ethical IT consultant?
options: Subscribes to a professional body which has a code of professional conduct
Acts as a guide or mentor to junior or less experienced consultants
Has professional indemnity and public liability insurance as necessary
Takes assignments in any field to maximise income
explain: An ethical consultant takes assignments only in those fields where they can confidently predict that they can help their client.

q: What does 'digital divide' refer to under social impacts?
options: Monitoring access to data on networks
explain: Digital divide: the haves and have-nots.

q: In research ethics, 'deception' means:
options: Withdrawing at any time without penalty
explain: deception - withholding information; consent - informing participants.

q: In research ethics, 'confidentiality' is to be handled in accordance with:
explain: confidentiality - in accordance with DPA/GDPR.

q: In research ethics, participants must be able to withdraw:
options: At any time, with a financial penalty
explain: withdrawal - at any time without penalty.

q: According to the lecture summary, ethics and morals are:
options: At times used interchangeably, but have two very different meanings
explain: Ethics and morals are at times used interchangeable, but have two very different meanings.

q: What should you do before you make an ethical decision?
options: Define the areas of potential conflict
Ask your peer group to decide for you
List the consequences of the actions
explain: Slide 8 lists these five steps, after which you make the decision.

q: What are the main responsibilities of an ethical consultant in IT?
options: Subscribes to a professional body which has a code of professional conduct
Charges clients according to their degree classification
Is professionally qualified in these areas and keeps up their CPD
Accepts any assignment offered by a client
Takes assignments only in fields where they can confidently predict they can help their client
Has professional indemnity and public liability insurance as necessary
explain: These match the slide's list of ethical consultant traits.

q: Which statements describe an ethical consultant in IT?
options: Subscribes to a professional body which has a code of professional conduct
Is professionally qualified in these areas and keeps up their CPD
Has professional indemnity and public liability insurance as necessary
Takes assignments only in fields where they can confidently predict they can help their client
Acts as a guide or mentor to junior or less experienced consultants
Supports their professional body with their time or 'pro bono' consulting as appropriate
explain: All six bullets on the slide describe the ethical consultant.

q: Which of the following are listed as potential areas of ethical conflict (ethical pressures)?
explain: Potential areas for conflict: self, manager, client, organization, family, peer group.

q: Which of the following are basic concepts in ethical decisions?
explain: Slide 9 lists Responsibility, Accountability, Liability, Due Process, Legal Principle.

q: Which of the following does the lecture give as sources of ethics?
explain: Where do ethics come from? Supernaturalism, Intuitionism, Consequentialism, Exemplars, Ideologies.

q: Which statements about ethics are correct?
options: Ethos is Greek for custom or character
Ethics are the same for everyone
Ethics are not the same for everyone
Ethics are not necessarily the law
Ethics are only about written rules
explain: Slides 3 and 4.

q: When participants are involved in research, which issues must be considered?
explain: Slide 24 lists consent, deception, withdrawal, confidentiality, protection.

q: Which of the following are listed as social impacts of IT?
options: Digital divide: the haves and have-nots
Monitoring access to data on networks
Quality: how good is good enough?
explain: Social impacts: Quality, Employment, Digital divide. Software theft is under IPR; the others under Privacy.

q: Which of the following are listed under the privacy issue in IT?
options: Monitoring access to data on networks
explain: Privacy: Big Brother (data mining, web surveillance, facial recognition, customer profiling); Your boss is watching (monitoring access).

q: Which of the following are listed under intellectual property rights as ethical issues in IT?
options: Copyright, ownership, how to reward the authors
explain: Intellectual Property Rights: copyright, ownership, how to reward the authors; software theft, illicit copying, spurious backups.

q: Which are listed as personal values in business ethics?
explain: Personal values include integrity, honesty, quality, loyalty, professionalism, responsibility, mutual respect, fairness and meritocracy, leadership, client focus and teamwork.

q: Which pairings of ethical position and statement are correct?
options: Moral realism - 'it is wrong to murder'
explain: Slide 11 gives all four pairings.

q: Which pairings of ethical position and statement are correct?
explain: Subjectivism = 'I disapprove of murder'; Prescriptivism = 'don't murder'; Emotivism = 'down with murder'; moral realism = 'it is wrong to murder'.

q: Which outcomes in the prisoner theory game are correct?
options: Both betray: both are set free
Both silent: each serves two years
A betrays, B silent: A is set free and B serves three years
Both silent: each serves one year
A betrays, B silent: A serves one year
Both betray: each serves two years
explain: Slide 15 gives the three outcomes.

q: Which statements about prisoner theory are correct?
options: Purely rational people will betray the other
Betrayal is never the outcome for rational people
Both could get a lower sentence if both stay silent
The detainees can communicate with each other
Two completely rational people might not cooperate
The decision will affect the detainees' future reputation
explain: Detainees are in solitary confinement and the decision will not affect their reputation; rational people (looking out for #1) betray.

q: Which of the following are rules or principles for ethical decisions given in the lecture?
explain: Slide 9 lists these four.

q: Business ethics involves adhering to which of the following?
explain: Business ethics involves adhering to legal, regulatory, professional and company standards, keeping promises, commitments and abiding by general principles like fairness, truth, honesty and respect.

q: Which definitions of ethics are given for 'ethos'?
options: Law: rules that mandate or prohibit behaviour
Science: the moral element determining a character's action rather than his/her thought or emotion
Policy: guidelines with penalties for non-compliance
Philosophy: science of the character of a group or individual
Sociology: underlying sentiment informing beliefs, customs, practices
explain: Slide 3 gives sociology, philosophy and science definitions.
